what: Mosaic mines and processes crop nutrients. It digs phosphate rock in Florida and potash in Saskatchewan and New Mexico, turns them into fertilizer, and sells it to farmers worldwide. It also has a large distribution and blending business in Brazil.
customers: Farmers, through agricultural retailers and cooperatives, plus industrial buyers of phosphate products. Prices are set by global commodity markets.
money: Processed phosphate fertilizers from Florida and Louisiana operations.
Potash from Canadian and US mines, sold globally.
Blending, distribution and retail of crop nutrients in Brazil.
moat: Fertilizer mines are irreplaceable assets: there are only a handful of economic potash basins and phosphate deposits in the world, permitting new ones takes a decade, and Mosaic owns some of the best. The Brazilian distribution network adds something rarer still, direct access to the fastest-growing agricultural market, which pure miners lack.
risks: The trailing twelve months show a net loss of about $1.1B and free cash flow of roughly negative $808.3M.
Fertilizer prices collapsed from the 2022 spike: revenue went from $19.1B to $11.1B before recovering to $12.1B, and the earnings swing was far larger than the revenue swing.
Debt of $5.2B against $276.6M of cash is heavy for a company currently losing money.
Phosphate production in Florida carries large environmental liabilities, including the long-term cost of gypsum stacks and water management.
Brazilian operations add currency risk and have been less profitable than the mining assets.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 0.53 times sales, which is a price for a company the market expects to keep losing money.
Potash and phosphate are consumed every season and cannot be substituted: crop yields fall without them, which puts a floor under long-run demand.
Supply is concentrated and new capacity is slow and expensive, so prices recover sharply when inventories clear.
Eighteen analysts average a $25.16 target, about 27% above the current price.
watch: Phosphate and potash prices against Mosaic’s cash cost per tonne. This is a commodity producer: the spread between the two explains nearly all the variation in earnings, and nothing management does matters as much.
view: Fertilizer is one of the purest commodity cycles in the market, and Mosaic is a leveraged bet on it. That is not a criticism, it is the whole description. In 2022, when grain prices spiked and Russian and Belarusian supply was disrupted, Mosaic earned enormous money and the stock trebled. Three years later revenue has fallen by more than a third from that peak, the company is posting a trailing net loss of $1.1 billion, free cash flow is negative $808 million, and the shares trade at half of annual sales. Nothing about the assets has changed. Only the price of what comes out of them.

What makes this cycle worth paying attention to rather than ignoring is the supply side. You cannot respond to high fertilizer prices by building a potash mine; it takes the better part of a decade and billions of dollars, and the number of economic deposits on earth is small enough to list. Phosphate is similar, with the added complication that the environmental permitting in Florida is punishing. So capacity does not arrive when prices are high, and it does not leave when prices are low — it just sits there, producing, until demand catches up. Meanwhile farmers can defer a season of application but not two, because yields fall and they can see it in the field. That combination is what historically turns fertilizer troughs into violent recoveries.

The reason to be careful is the balance sheet rather than the cycle. $5.2 billion of debt against $277 million of cash, while losing money and burning cash, is a position that works fine if the recovery comes within a couple of years and becomes genuinely uncomfortable if it does not. This is the standard mistake in commodity investing: being right about the cycle and wrong about the timing, in a company that needed you to be right about both. I would also discount the Brazilian distribution business, which sounds strategic and has consistently earned less than the mines.

So: a real asset, a real cycle, a trough valuation, and a balance sheet that removes the margin for error. At 0.53 times sales this is priced as though the current depressed margins are permanent, which in a business with no new supply coming is unlikely to be true. But it is a position to size for the possibility that nothing happens for two more years. If you want the same cycle with less balance-sheet risk, Nutrien and CF are the comparisons to run first. The number to watch is not Mosaic’s earnings, which will be noise, but the phosphate and potash price against the company’s own stated cash cost per tonne.
bull: Inventories clear, prices recover into a market where no new mine can arrive for a decade, and operating leverage on an unchanged asset base turns a $1.1 billion loss into large profits.
bear: Grain prices stay weak, farmers keep deferring application, and a company with $5.2 billion of debt and negative cash flow has to finance its way through two more years of trough pricing.
